For Ricardo & Julie · 25 October 2026

Three cities,
five doors.

Cape Town, the Algarve and Rhodes — forty-five properties priced, five chosen, and the plain answer to where the company should live.

Prepared by Bruce WaynePrices read 25 October 2026Research, not advice
The short version

What this document says, in five lines

This is the family version of three weeks of research. The detail lives in the three reports behind it — this is the part that answers the question we actually asked: where does the next property go, in whose name, and why.

Read these five and you have read the report

  1. Cape Town wins on money. The Obs Court two-bed returns 11.2% net on every rand it takes to buy and furnish, and about R62 000 a year after tax for every R1 million invested — more than either European city pays today.
  2. Europe wins on currency and on the life we want. The Algarve's 7.5% is in euros, and the rand has slid 3.3% a year against the euro for twenty years. In rand terms those two numbers arrive at almost the same place — but only one of them is money we can spend in Europe.
  3. Rhodes is the smallest door and the most strategic. €87 036 buys a finished two-bed that pays 7.1%. It is also the property that turns Julie's Greek residency from a plan into an address.
  4. Put the bricks in our own names, not in a company. Personal names earn 15.9% in Cape Town against 13.6% through a company. In Portugal the individual pays 8.75% where a company chain pays 28%. The Greek company only starts winning above roughly €26 000–€41 000 of rent per property.
  5. The biggest tax decision is not the country of the company — it is the country we live in. While we are South African resident, SARS taxes the profit at up to 45% and credits whatever Greece or Portugal already took. Moving residence is worth more than every structure in this document combined. Nothing else comes close.

How we looked

Forty-five properties, one model, no brochures

Every listing below was live on the day it was read. Every price is an asking price or a court floor — not a sold price. Every return is computed on one identical model so the three cities can be compared without flattering any of them.

  • Rent. Measured, not quoted: live Airbnb medians for the same two-bedroom, four-guest, whole-home search in each city, for one peak week and one low week, then blended at the occupancy the data supports.
  • Costs. Platform fees, co-host and turnarounds, cleaning, utilities, guest supplies, linen, repairs, insurance, rates and levies — the full bill, not the rent.
  • Purchase. Transfer tax or IMT as it stands in 2026, notary and registration, works, furniture, and the licence.
  • Tax. Both ways: as an individual and through a company, with the exit included. This is where the three cities stop looking alike.
  • Currency. €1 = R18.5777, the European Central Bank rate on 23 October 2026.

The one thing to hold on to

Net yield is the honest measure: what is left after every cost, divided by everything it took to own the place. It is not the same as the rent divided by the price, which is the number brochures use and which flatters every property by about a third.

The three cities

What each one is actually for

Cape Town. Photograph: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Cape Town — the engine room

Fifteen two-bedroom properties, five auctions, five fixer-uppers and five new builds, from Muizenberg to Bloubergstrand. The range of outcomes is wider here than anywhere else we looked: 3.3% net at the bottom, 11.4% at the top, and the difference is almost never the building — it is the suburb and the price per square metre paid for it.

The city's short-let market is the deepest of the three, the finance is local and cheap relative to Europe, and the money comes back in the currency we spend every day. That is the case for Cape Town, and it is a strong one. The case against is equally clear: a draft by-law that moves heavy short-letting onto commercial rates from July 2027, sectional-title buildings that can ban it outright, and a rand that has lost nearly half its value against the euro in twenty years.

The Algarve — the euro we will actually spend

Fifteen properties across the Faro district: five judicial auctions, five village fixer-uppers and five new builds. Only one of the fifteen cleared a 7% net yield, and it was not the pretty one on the beachfront — it was a house behind Quarteira that needs €90 000 of work and sits three kilometres from the sand.

That is the lesson of this coast. The Algarve is priced for the view, and the view does not pay. What pays is buying a building at a court floor, spending real money on it once, and letting it as a whole home to people who want a house rather than a hotel room. The new builds on the coast are the worst of the three groups on return, and the village houses are the best — provided the works are costed honestly.

The other thing that matters here is not money: a short-let licence in Portugal is permanent and travels with the property. In a municipality that has frozen new registrations — a containment zone — a house with a live licence is worth more than the same house without one, and buying without one is buying a long-let at short-let prices.

Rhodes — the foothold

Fifteen listings again: five court auctions, five restoration projects and five new builds, from €54 000 to €389 000. What makes Rhodes different is not the yield — it is the price of entry. An €87 000 all-in flat is a door we can open without a bond, a currency bet or a committee.

Greece is also the one country where the tax rule is genuinely hostile to a small non-resident landlord: a non-resident individual is taxed on turnover, less a flat 5% allowance, with no deduction for the cleaning, the co-host or the utilities. At €13 000 of rent that hurts. At €60 000 it is the reason to own through a company instead — the crossover is about €30 000 of rent per company, which is two flats or one large villa.

And there is a dated lever here that exists nowhere else: from 1 July 2027 Greece has signalled a 15.45% transfer tax for non-EU individual buyers, against 3.09% today. It does not touch us — a Portuguese passport is an EU passport — but it tells you what the direction of travel is for everyone else in the queue.

The top five

Five doors, and what each one honestly pays

Chosen on net yield after every cost, the ten-year return, how much capital they tie up, and whether we could actually get them. Two in Cape Town because that is where the money is; two in the Algarve because that is where the euro is; one in Rhodes because it is the cheapest way to own a piece of Greece.

The whole set, if we bought it tomorrow

All five, everything in, is R15 293 694. They would throw off about R1 242 780 a year after each country's own tax, and R774 773 after South African tax — 8.1% and 5.1% on the money. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy all five. The point of the number is scale: this is what the whole idea costs, and it is a house, not a portfolio.

The numbers, side by side

Same tax basis, three different cities

The three cities look like 11.2%, 7.5% and 7.1% — until you put them on the same tax basis. The gap closes to almost nothing, and that is the finding that decides this document.

Net yield on everything it costs to own — before and after South African tax

The Portuguese and Greek numbers in the three source reports were computed as a non-resident individual would be taxed there. We are South African resident, so SARS taxes the profit at up to 45% and credits what the foreign country already took. Once that is applied to all three, they land within 1.3 points of each other: Cape Town 6.2%, Rhodes 5.1%, the Algarve 4.9%.

Which means the choice is not "where is the highest yield". It is "which currency, which risk, and which life" — because the tax bill is the same shape in all three while we live in South Africa. (Every figure here assumes the top marginal rate of 45%. At 41% each European line improves by about 0.5 of a point and Cape Town by the same, so the ranking does not change.)

What one million rand earns a year after tax, today and after a change of residence

This is the chart that should decide things. Per million rand invested, Cape Town pays R61 702 a year after tax; Rhodes R51 116; the Algarve R49 085. Cease South African residence and the European two climb by 40–50% — while Cape Town, being South African source income either way, does not move at all.

The currency question, in three sentences

€1 bought R9.63 in October 2006 and buys R18.58 today. That is 3.34% a year of rand weakness compounded — 2.13% a year over the last ten. So a 7.5% euro yield is worth roughly 11.1% in rand terms if the slide continues at its twenty-year pace, and a euro flat is a hedge that pays for itself in the currency we will spend it in.

That is a description of the past, not a forecast. It is also the single assumption in this report most likely to be wrong in any given year — which is exactly why we should not hold only one currency.

Where the company should live

You already own the right passport. Do not buy a structure to go with it.

The research behind this section is the hardest in the set: Cyprus, Estonia, Georgia, Singapore, Malta, Greece, Portugal, Spain and South Africa, from primary sources. The conclusion is shorter than the research.

Here is the fact that decides it. Greece taxes the profit on a Greek property at 22% whoever owns it. Portugal taxes a Portuguese property at 20% whoever owns it. A Cypriot, Estonian or Singapore company above a Greek flat does not change either line by a single euro — it changes only what happens to the money after Greece or Portugal has taken its share. So the holding country is not a tax-rate decision. It is a decision about four things: the exit, the deferral, the succession, and the annual cost.

And while we are South African resident, one more fact sits above all four: section 9D of the Income Tax Act looks straight through any foreign company more than 50% held by South African residents and taxes its profit in our hands at up to 45% — whether or not a dividend is ever paid. A passive Cyprus company with nominee directors is transparent to SARS. The deferral it looks like it gives us does not exist.

What the state takes, on €30 000 of rent and €11 000 of costs

Read the first and last lines together. Same flat, same tenant, same rent — the difference is where we live, and it is worth about €5,925 a year on one property. No structure in this document, at any price, buys that.

So: personal names, and one company that stays in its lane

  • Cape Town, in your own name. RR2 178 486 through a company comes out at 13.6% a year after tax against 15.9% in your own name, adds about R120 000 more in accounting and audit over a decade, and gains nothing on exit — SARS treats shares in a residential property company as property, so selling the company instead of the flat does not escape the transfer duty.
  • The Algarve, in your own name. 8.75% of gross as a non-resident individual, against 28% through a Portuguese company owned from abroad. The company never catches up here at any size — the individual wins every property on this coast.
  • Rhodes, in Julie's name once her Greek residence is real, and in your own name before that. A company loses on all fifteen listings at these ticket sizes; the Greek crossover is roughly €26 000–€41 000 of rent per company, depending on the property's value. At €13 000 it is a €5 000-a-year subscription the rent cannot carry.
  • The South African property company stays exactly where it is — on South African property. Do not let it buy the Algarve or Rhodes bricks. A South African company pays 27% and then 20% dividends tax to get the cash to us — 41.6% of the profit, against 45% for us personally, so it saves almost nothing; it adds about R120 000 more in accounting than holding the property personally; it loses the individual's capital gains treatment; and no Greek or Portuguese bank will lend it money. If instead it buys through a foreign subsidiary, section 9D taxes us at 45% anyway. It is a good vehicle for South African assets and a bad one for foreign ones.
  • No Cyprus holding company and no Maltese foundation — not yet. The pair cost €15 000–€20 000 a year, buy no tax benefit while we are South African resident, and matter only at three or more properties or once residence changes. Building it now would be a €20 000-a-year ornament.

What we would build instead — and it is cheaper

Own each property in a personal name, in the country where it stands. Put one will in place, governed by one law, chosen deliberately — South African law gives us freedom to leave our assets as we choose, while a Portuguese will cannot override the fixed share Portuguese law reserves for the children. That single choice is worth more than any company, and it costs a few hundred euros.

The passports we already hold

Citizenship is the cheapest structure in the file

Three citizenships in this family, and each one is worth money at a specific moment in the purchase. None of them needs an offshore company to work.

Your Portuguese citizenship

An EU passport is the largest single financial asset in this report, and it is already in the drawer.

  • Greece, 3.09% not 15.45%. The signalled July 2027 step-up applies to non-EU individuals. On a €400 000 Greek property that is €49 440 avoided; on the €87 036 Archangelos flat, about €7 900.
  • Portugal, resident scale not the 7.5% flat. As a Portuguese tax resident, IMT at €255 000 on the resident scale is 4.63% instead of 7.5% — €7 311 saved on the Benfarras house.
  • No Golden Visa needed. Greek residence by investment in Rhodes means €800 000 in one property of at least 120 m² — and the €87 036 flat, at 67 m², would not even qualify. EU citizenship already gives us what the visa sells, without locking eight hundred thousand euros into one villa.

Julie's Greek citizenship and residence

This is the piece that makes the Greek property work rather than merely exist.

  • First-time buyer transfer tax 1.41% instead of 3.09% — small on a €64 000 flat (about €900), material on anything larger.
  • Taxed on profit, not turnover. A Greek resident deducts the real costs of letting; a non-resident cannot. On €30 000 of rent that difference is worth roughly €2 000–€3 000 a year, every year.
  • The only honest route to a Greek company. If the rent roll ever justifies an IKE, a resident director and a real office are what make it defensible against section 9D — substance is the defence, not paperwork.
  • The cost to weigh: a Greek tax resident is taxed by Greece on worldwide income, at rates up to 44%. It is only sensible if her other income is modest and the family plan is genuinely Greek.

Your South African citizenship

Home, the company, and the reason the tax rate is 45% while we stay. Worth keeping — but see it for what it is: the biggest tax line in the whole study.

If ceasing South African tax residence ever becomes the plan, it must happen before the property build-up, not after: ceasing residence triggers an exit charge on worldwide assets, and assets bought afterwards sit outside it.

Which leaves the real question

Not "which country should own the company", but "where do we intend to be tax resident in five years". If the answer is South Africa, everything above is about clean ownership, asset protection and succession — not tax. If the answer is Portugal or Greece, the company layer becomes genuinely valuable and the order of operations changes.

One decision, worth about €5,925 a year per property. We do not need to answer it today. We do need to stop pretending a structure can answer it for us.

The risks that actually bite

Five things that cost more than the tax rate

  • Auctions take no prisoners. No bond clause, no cooling-off, deposit on the fall of the hammer. Four of our five are auctions, and every one of them needs the money ready before the day rather than after it. If the deposit is not in place, we do not bid.
  • The licence, not the promise. Cape Town's draft by-law moves heavy short-letting onto commercial rates from July 2027. Portugal's containment zones let a council refuse new short-let registrations outright. Greece requires an AMA number per property under Law 5170/2025. A property without the right registration is a long-let at short-let prices — the most expensive mistake on this list.
  • The building can ban it. Most sectional-title schemes in Cape Town may prohibit short-letting outright. Obs Court already allows it — that must be in writing, and confirmed by the trustees, before any deposit moves.
  • The platforms report us. Under DAC7, Airbnb and Booking hand our gross rents to the Greek and Portuguese tax authorities automatically. The Greek gross-basis regime and the Portuguese simplified regime are enforced against platform numbers, not our own accounts.
  • Occupancy carries the model. Every number here runs at the occupancy the data supports — 46% in Cape Town, 42–45% in Greece, and a stabilised year in Portugal. On the winning Cape Town unit the range from 6.5% to 17.3% net is set by nights and nightly rate, not by the interest rate. That spread is the risk.
What happens next

By dependency, not by date

Nothing here needs a diary. Each step needs the one before it to be true first. Everything inside a step can run in parallel.

1
Answer the residence question, on paper. South Africa for the next five years, or not? One paragraph, written down. Every number in this report is downstream of it, and no purchase should happen until it is answered.
2
Get the Cape Town building's rules in writing. Trustees' consent to short-letting and the levy schedule, before either Obs Court unit is bid on. This is the cheapest possible way to lose a deposit.
3
Be ready for 12 November. If the 515 Obs Court hammer lands under R1.90 million, it is the better buy of the two and the money must already be in place. If it does not, buy the 73 m² unit at R1.995 million and be done.
4
Have the Algarve watched, not chased. The Benfarras lot closed on 21 October, so it is our benchmark: a Loulé-district house, bought at a court floor, three kilometres from the beach, at a 7% net hurdle or better. Sítio das Benfarras sets the price we bid to on the next one.
5
Decide Rhodes in Julie's name, not ours. The 27 November Archangelos auction is worth taking only if her Greek residence is real or imminent — because the resident route is what makes the Greek tax arithmetic work. If it is not, we wait; there will be another €64 000 flat.
6
Put the will in place before the third deed. One will, one governing law, chosen deliberately and seen by advisers in each country. A few hundred euros against the most expensive outcome in the file.
7
Revisit the structure at three properties, not before. That is when a family layer earns its €6 000 a year. Until then it is decoration, and decoration does not pay a bond.
